title: Ἀρότης καὶ λύκος
part: The Ploughman and the Wolf (Chambry 64 · Perry 38)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 64 (= Perry 38). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀρότης λύσας τὸ ζεῦγος ἐπὶ ποτὸν ἀπῆγε· λύκος δὲ λιμώττων καὶ τροφὴν ζητῶν, ὡς περιέτυχε τῷ ἀρότρῳ, τὸ μὲν πρῶτον τὰς τῶν ταύρων ζεύγλας περιέλειχε, λαθὼν δὲ κατὰ μικρόν, ἐπειδὴ καθῆκε τὸν αὐχένα, ἀνασπᾶν μὴ δυνάμενος, ἐπὶ τὴν ἄρουραν τὸ ἄροτρον ἔσυρεν.
sentences.tr: Arotēs lysas to zeugos epi poton apēge· lykos de limōttōn kai trophēn zētōn, hōs perietyche tōi arotrōi, to men prōton tas tōn taurōn zeuglas perieleiche, lathōn de kata mikron, epeidē kathēke ton auchena, anaspan mē dynamenos, epi tēn arouran to arotron esyren.
sentences.l: A ploughman, having unyoked his team, was leading it off to drink; and a wolf, being hungry and seeking food, when he came upon the plough, at first licked round the yoke-straps of the oxen, but little by little, without noticing it, when he had let his neck down into them, not being able to pull it up again, he dragged the plough over the field.
sentences.i: A ploughman unyoked his team and led it off to water; and a wolf, hungry and looking for food, came upon the plough and at first licked round the oxen's yoke-straps — then little by little, before he knew it, he had let his neck down into them, and, unable to draw it out again, went dragging the plough across the field.
sentences.n: A chain of participles carries the action: λύσας hangs on ἀπῆγε, while λιμώττων, ζητῶν (present) and λαθών (aorist), δυνάμενος (present) hang on ἔσυρεν at the end. ζεύγλη is the loop of the yoke that goes round an ox's neck; the wolf licks it for the sweat and grease. λαθών on its own usually means 'unnoticed, secretly'; here, with no one about to notice, it is most naturally taken of the wolf himself — before he knew it — though the reflexive sense is normally spelled out with a pronoun.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἀρότης ἐπανελθὼν καὶ θεασάμενος αὐτὸν ἔλεγεν· « Εἴθε γάρ, ὦ κακὴ κεφαλή, καταλιπὼν τὰς ἁρπαγὰς καὶ τὸ ἀδικεῖν ἐπὶ τὸ γεωπονεῖν τραπείης. »
sentences.tr: Ho de arotēs epanelthōn kai theasamenos auton elegen· « Eithe gar, ō kakē kephalē, katalipōn tas harpagas kai to adikein epi to geōponein trapeiēs. »
sentences.l: And the ploughman, having come back and having caught sight of him, said: « If only, you wicked head, having left off your robberies and your wrongdoing, you would turn to working the land. »
sentences.i: The ploughman came back, saw him, and said: « Would that you might give up your robbery and your wrongdoing, you villain, and turn to farming! »
sentences.n: Now εἴθε with the aorist optative (τραπείης) — a wish for the future that could still come true, against the impossible wish with the indicative in the fable before. ὦ κακὴ κεφαλή, 'wicked head', is standing Greek abuse where English says 'you villain'. τὸ ἀδικεῖν and τὸ γεωπονεῖν are articular infinitives: wrongdoing and land-working turned into nouns by the article.

sentences.t: Οὕτως οἱ πονηροὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, κἂν χρηστότητα ἐπαγγέλλωνται, διὰ τὸν τρόπον οὐ πιστεύονται.
sentences.tr: Houtōs hoi ponēroi tōn anthrōpōn, kan chrēstotēta epangellōntai, dia ton tropon ou pisteuontai.
sentences.l: So the wicked among men, even if they profess honesty, are not believed, because of their character.
sentences.n: κἄν is καὶ ἐάν by crasis, 'even if', taking the subjunctive. διὰ τὸν τρόπον: their known way of behaving is what discredits the profession. The moral opens with plain οὕτως, not the commoner οὕτω καί.
